statement: In a systematic review of 48 studies (1,774 people) of psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT and mescaline, mostly given in laboratories, clinical trials or ceremonies with preparation and aftercare (Evens et al., 2023; AMSTAR 2 critically low), measurements taken between one day and one month after use, compared with each person's own measurements before, most often showed less depression and stress and more wellbeing, mindfulness and social connectedness (changes reported in 70 to 90% of the studies that measured these), and no study found group-level worsening of mental health. Bad after-effects were reported in 14 of the 25 studies that said they looked for them: mostly headaches (52 people, usually lasting a day or two), then sleep problems, tension and exhaustion, with single cases of severe anxiety and of relapse to methamphetamine use. Half the studies had a control group of some kind, but only 14 of the 48 had a placebo group with double-blinding, only statistically significant results were counted, and half the studies did not say whether they looked for side effects, so the size and cause of these changes, and how often they happen with recreational use, are unknown. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: A review of 48 studies found that in the days and weeks after taking a psychedelic, people often felt less depressed and stressed and more connected, compared with before. Some had headaches or slept badly, and a few had serious anxiety. Most studies had no comparison group and took place with support around them, so we do not know how big or how common these changes are in everyday use.
population: Adults, clinical and nonclinical, taking classic psychedelics in laboratory studies, clinical trials or ceremonies, in 48 studies gathered by a systematic review
exposure: A session with psilocybin, ayahuasca or DMT, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT or mescaline
comparator: The same people's measurements before the session (a control group in 24 studies, placebo-controlled and double-blind in 14)
outcome: Psychological measures and adverse effects between one day and one month after use
magnitude: No effect sizes; counts of studies. Changes in 70 to 90% of studies measuring depression, stress and grief; mindfulness; personality and attitudes; wellbeing; social effects. Adverse events: assessed or mentioned in 25 of 48 studies (550 participants); none in 11 (297 participants); reported in 14 (253 participants): 52 headaches, 6 sleep disturbances, 6 tension, 3 exhaustion, 3 visual distortion, single severe cases.

evidence.locator: Results › Study selection and sample characteristics, 1st paragraph; Results › Risk of bias, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: 48 studies (52 publications), 1774 participants: 16 psilocybin, 16 ayahuasca, 10 LSD, 2 5-MeO-DMT, 3 several, 1 mescaline; sample sizes 6 to 315 (median 18). 14 studies (29%) had a standardized treatment, placebo control and double-blind allocation; 19 (40%) a standardized treatment but no control group and/or no double-blind allocation; 15 (31%) no standardized treatment (e.g. observational studies).

Changes were observed most consistently (in 70 to 90% of studies investigating the domain, more than 450 participants each) for depression, stress and grief; mindfulness, acceptance and emotion regulation; personality, values and attitudes; wellbeing; and social effects. At group level no worsening of psychopathology was reported, and there was no evidence of increases in suicidality, manic or psychotic symptoms or of decreases in cognitive performance, though few studies assessed these.

25 studies (52%, 550 participants) mentioned whether they assessed adverse events; 11 (297 participants) reported none; 14 (253 participants) reported 52 headaches (usually lasting no longer than a day or two), 6 insomnia or sleep disturbances, 6 tension, 3 exhaustion, 3 visual distortion, 2 each of fatigue, migraine, nausea, difficulty concentrating and vivid dreams, and single cases including severe anxiety exacerbation with methamphetamine relapse and a psychiatric disturbance lasting one week.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Risk of bias, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: 72% of studies lacked a control group, double-blind allocation or standardized treatment; only statistically significant effects were summarized; settings with preparation and aftercare mean the results cannot be generalized to recreational use, and selective reporting or publication bias may contribute; the authors present the results as effects observed under favourable conditions, not the average expected effect.

risk_of_bias.note: Mostly uncontrolled pre–post studies, vote counting of significant results, selective adverse-event reporting; review not appraised for bias (AMSTAR 2 critically low).

indirectness.note: Supportive settings, not recreational use; several different psychedelics combined.

publication_bias.note: Possible, as the authors say; already reflected in the rating.

grade.reasoning: Most included studies are pre–post or observational, so the evidence starts low; rated down for risk of bias and indirectness to very low. Worded as an association with before-use measurements. Status replicated: many studies in the same direction for the main domains, though of mixed design.
